concept.name: Garbage Collection Algorithms

relationships.description: Connects Garbage Collection Algorithms to jvm internals and garbage collection in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Automated memory reclamation strategies—spanning tracing (mark-sweep, copying, generational/regional) and reference counting—that trade throughput, heap overhead, and pause-time predictability.
spark.keyTakeaway: Modern low-latency collectors (ZGC, Shenandoah, Go's tri-color GC) eliminate multi-second pauses by doing marking and compaction concurrently via read/write barriers.

concept.whyItMatters: Manual `malloc`/`free` risks use-after-free vulnerabilities and memory leaks, while naive stop-the-world (STW) garbage collection freezes application threads for seconds under heavy allocation. Understanding tracing vs. reference counting, generational hypotheses, and tri-color write/load barriers lets you size heaps, tune `GOGC`/`GOMEMLIMIT` or JVM flags, and eliminate p99 tail-latency spikes.
whenToUse: Choose **generational copying/regional GC (G1GC, V8 Orinoco)** for general server workloads with high short-lived allocation rates (90%+ objects die in Eden) needing high throughput.
Choose **concurrent compacting GC (JVM ZGC, Shenandoah)** when p99.9 latency SLAs demand <1 ms GC pauses even on 10 GB–1 TB+ heaps.

Choose **reference counting + cycle detector (CPython, Swift ARC)** when deterministic immediate destruction (RAII for file handles/sockets) and minimal heap headroom matter more than raw multithreaded throughput.
whenNotToUse: Hard real-time systems (e.g., audio DSP, flight control, <50 µs jitter budgets) where even brief STW barrier safepoints or allocation stalls violate deterministic deadlines—use arena/region allocators or Rust ownership.
Memory-constrained embedded devices with <1.5x live-set RAM headroom, because tracing collectors degrade into continuous CPU thrashing as free heap approaches 0%.
Tightly packed off-heap/GPU buffers where object-header and pointer-chasing overhead destroys SIMD throughput.
keyPoints: The **Weak Generational Hypothesis** observes that >90% of allocated objects die young; copying live survivors out of Eden into Survivor/Old space takes time proportional *only* to live bytes (`O(Live)`), not dead garbage.

Tracing collectors maintain the **tri-color invariant** (`White` = unvisited, `Grey` = discovered/unscanned, `Black` = scanned/live); concurrent mutators require **write barriers** (SATB in G1GC or Dijkstra/hybrid in Go) so a `Black` object never points to a `White` object without re-greying.
**Reference counting** reclaims acyclic garbage immediately at zero pause cost, but fails on reference cycles (`A <-> B`) and incurs atomic `inc`/`dec` cache-line contention on shared pointers.

**ZGC (JDK 21+ Generational ZGC)** uses 64-bit colored pointers and load barriers to relocate objects concurrently while application threads run, keeping STW pauses under ~250 µs regardless of heap size.
Go's non-compacting concurrent tri-color mark-sweep trades compaction for simplicity, using `GOGC` (default 100%, triggering at 2x live heap) and `GOMEMLIMIT` to prevent container OOMs.

examples.title: JVM Latency Migration: G1GC to Generational ZGC
examples.scenario: A Java payment-gateway microservice with a 32 GB heap and 1.5 GB/s allocation rate experiences 180–450 ms p999 pauses during G1GC mixed evacuations.
examples.outcome: Switching to `-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational` (JDK 21+) moves object relocation and reference remapping into concurrent load barriers, dropping p999 GC pauses to <0.4 ms at a ~5–10% throughput/CPU cost.

examples.title: Go Container OOM Prevention with `GOMEMLIMIT`
examples.scenario: A Go service in a 2 GiB Kubernetes pod has a 1.1 GiB live heap; with `GOGC=100`, the next GC cycle doesn't trigger until 2.2 GiB, causing the Linux kernel OOM-killer to terminate the pod.
examples.outcome: Setting `GOMEMLIMIT=1700MiB` (Go 1.19+) forces the runtime to run GC cycles earlier as heap approaches 1.7 GiB without disabling `GOGC=100` pacing under normal load.

tradeOffs.pro: Stop-the-world Parallel/Throughput GC maximizes CPU cycles for application work (~98%+ mutator utilization) with zero barrier overhead.
tradeOffs.con: Causes multi-hundred-millisecond or multi-second freezes on multi-gigabyte heaps.

tradeOffs.factor: Heap Headroom vs. GC CPU Frequency
tradeOffs.pro: Generous heap headroom (2x–3x live set) lets tracing collectors amortize mark work over long intervals.
tradeOffs.con: Tightening heap limits below ~1.3x live set triggers back-to-back GC cycles (GC thrashing) or allocation stalls.

tradeOffs.pro: Copying/compacting collectors (G1, ZGC) eliminate external fragmentation and enable fast bump-pointer allocation.
tradeOffs.con: Non-compacting collectors (Go, classic Mark-Sweep) avoid relocation barriers but rely on size-classed `tcmalloc`-style spans to bound fragmentation.

failureModes.name: Evacuation Failure / Allocation Stall
failureModes.description: Mutator threads allocate faster than the concurrent collector can mark and reclaim regions (G1GC `to-space exhausted` or ZGC allocation stall), triggering a fallback full STW GC or blocking mutators.
failureModes.mitigation: Increase heap headroom, reduce per-request temporary object churn, or increase concurrent GC threads (`-XX:ConcGCThreads`).

failureModes.name: Unbounded Reference Cycles / Retained Listener Leaks
failureModes.description: A long-lived cache, static map, or unclosed listener holds references to short-lived objects—no GC algorithm can collect reachable memory, causing steady heap growth to OOM.
failureModes.mitigation: Profile live-set dominator trees (`jcmd GC.heap_dump`, `pprof heap`) and break unintended strong references with weak references (`WeakReference`, `weakref`).

failureModes.name: Finalizer / Native Off-Heap Exhaustion
failureModes.description: Objects wrapping large native buffers (e.g., `DirectByteBuffer`, JNI allocations) look tiny (32 bytes) to the JVM heap, so GC never triggers until OS native memory OOMs.
failureModes.mitigation: Explicitly close native resources (`try-with-resources`), cap `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize`, and avoid deprecated `finalize()` (which delays reclamation by 2+ cycles).

failureModes.name: CPython Reference-Count Thrashing & CoW Unsharing
failureModes.description: Forked worker processes (`gunicorn` pre-fork) touch Python objects whose `ob_refcnt` increments on every read, triggering Linux Copy-on-Write (CoW) page duplication across all workers.
failureModes.mitigation: Call `gc.freeze()` after master-process imports in Python 3.7+ or use `multiprocessing` / shared-nothing workers to preserve CoW memory pages.

commonMistakes: Setting `-Xms` and `-Xmx` too close to the live working set, starving the collector of free regions and causing 50%+ CPU spent in GC.
Disabling Python's cyclic `gc` completely without verifying zero circular references in frameworks, causing slow memory leaks.
Assuming Go's `GOGC=off` + `GOMEMLIMIT` prevents all OOMs—Go still allocates stack/runtime metadata and cannot reclaim below the live set.
Calling `System.gc()` in production hot paths, which forces a synchronous Stop-The-World full collection unless `-XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent` is set.
Over-tuning 15+ legacy JVM GC flags instead of measuring allocation rate (`MB/s`), live set size, and pause distribution first.

sections.content:
## The idea

Every automatic memory manager answers one question: **which heap objects are still reachable from GC roots** (thread stacks, CPU registers, global/static variables)? Two primary families exist:

1. **Direct (Reference Counting)**: Each object tracks an incoming-pointer count. When `refcount` hits `0`, memory is freed immediately. It is simple and incremental, but cannot free reference cycles (`A -> B -> A`) without a secondary tracing pass.
2. **Indirect (Tracing)**: Starting from GC roots, the collector traverses the object graph and marks everything reachable, then sweeps or copies away the rest. Because most objects die young (**Weak Generational Hypothesis**), modern tracing GCs partition the heap into Young and Old generations—collecting Young frequently in `O(Live_Young)` time via copying, and scanning Old infrequently.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a **concurrent tri-color mark-sweep** cycle (used by Go and the mark phase of G1GC) with `Root -> A -> B`:

1. **Initial STW (Mark Setup)**: Pause mutators briefly (~100 µs), enable the **write barrier**, and color `Root` and direct target `A` **Grey**.
2. **Concurrent Mark**: Collector pops `A` from the grey worklist, scans its fields, colors `B` **Grey**, and promotes `A` to **Black**.
3. **Mutator Race**: Before `B` is scanned, an application thread executes `A.child = C` (where `C` is **White**) and `B.ref = null`. Without a barrier, `A` (Black) would hide `C` (White) from the collector, causing a use-after-free bug!
4. **Write Barrier Save**: The write barrier intercepts `A.child = C`, shades `C` **Grey** (Dijkstra barrier) or shades overwritten `B` **Grey** (SATB), preserving the invariant that no Black object points directly to a White object.
5. **Mark Termination & Sweep**: Once the grey worklist drains, a brief STW (<200 µs) disables the barrier; remaining **White** objects are swept into free lists concurrently.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Barriers, card tables, and generational isolation
sections.content:
## Barriers, card tables, and generational isolation

Collecting the Young generation independently without scanning the entire 50 GB Old generation requires tracking **inter-generational pointers** (Old -> Young). Runtimes solve this with a **Card Table** (or Remembered Set): the heap is divided into 512-byte cards, each mapped to 1 byte in a flat array. Whenever a mutator writes a pointer into an Old object, a tiny post-write barrier sets its card byte dirty (`card[addr >> 9] = 0`).

During a Young GC, the collector only scans dirty cards instead of all 50 GB of Old Gen. In **Generational ZGC**, colored pointer metadata bits encode `Marked`, `Remapped`, and `Finalizable` states directly in unused upper virtual-address bits, allowing a 2-instruction load barrier to self-heal stale pointers on first read.

## Production collector comparison

| Collector / Runtime | Strategy | Compaction | Typical STW Pause | Sweet Spot |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **JVM G1GC** | Regional generational mark-copy | Yes (evacuation) | 10–200 ms | Balanced server throughput & latency |
| **JVM Gen ZGC** | Concurrent generational + load barriers | Yes (concurrent) | **<0.5 ms** | Ultra-low p999 latency, 4 GB–16 TB heaps |
| **Go Runtime GC** | Non-generational concurrent tri-color | No (size-classed spans) | 0.1–0.5 ms | Cloud-native services tuned via `GOGC` / `GOMEMLIMIT` |
| **CPython** | Refcounting + 3-gen cycle collector | No (pymalloc arenas) | ~1–10 ms (Gen 2) | Immediate resource cleanup, C-API interop |

## Failure modes

- **Allocation-rate outpacing collection**: If mutators allocate faster than concurrent marking finishes, G1 falls back to a multi-second Full STW GC, and Go forces mutators to perform **mark assists**, spiking request latency.
- **Humongous object fragmentation (G1GC)**: Objects larger than 50% of a G1 region (`1–32 MB`) bypass Eden and allocate directly into contiguous Old regions, fragmenting the heap.
- **Container cgroup OOM**: Leaving `GOGC=100` without `GOMEMLIMIT` or exceeding container RAM with JVM off-heap (`DirectByteBuffer` + metaspace + thread stacks) triggers Linux `SIGKILL` (`OOMKilled`).
- **Card-table false sharing**: High-concurrency threads mutating adjacent Old objects repeatedly dirty the same 64-byte cache line in the card table, throttling multicore scaling.

## Tuning methodology

Effective GC tuning follows three measurements rather than cargo-cult flags:
1. **Live Data Set (LDS)**: Measure heap occupancy immediately after a full collection. Size max heap to at least **2x–3x LDS** for tracing collectors.
2. **Allocation Rate (`MB/s`)**: High allocation rates (`>1 GB/s`) mean Eden fills every second; enlarging Young Gen or pooling hot buffers (e.g., Netty `ByteBuf`, Go `sync.Pool`) cuts GC frequency directly.
3. **Pause vs. CPU Budget**: If p999 tail latency is violated by evacuation pauses, switch to Generational ZGC/Shenandoah; if CPU is saturated by concurrent barriers, widen `GOGC` (e.g., `200`) or use Parallel/G1GC.

## Practical checklist

- Size container RAM limits to `Heap + Off-Heap/Metaspace + Thread Stacks + 20% OS headroom`.
- Set `GOMEMLIMIT` to ~80–85% of container memory in Go 1.19+ services.
- Enable `-Xlog:gc*` (JVM) or `GODEBUG=gctrace=1` (Go) in staging to verify live set size and allocation rate before tuning.
- Eliminate `finalize()` / heavy `Cleaner` chains on off-heap resources; close handles deterministically.
- Pool only large or expensive-to-initialize buffers (`sync.Pool` / `ByteBuf`); let Young Gen handle small short-lived objects.

interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Garbage Collection Algorithms. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?

nodes.label: Sweeper / Evacuator
nodes.role: Reclaim White or compact live regions

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Automated memory reclamation strategies—spanning tracing (mark-sweep, copying, generational/regional) and reference counting—that trade throughput, heap overhead, and pause-time predictability.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Tri-Color Marker applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Sweeper / Evacuator.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Sweeper / Evacuator experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Increase heap headroom, reduce per-request temporary object churn, or increase concurrent GC threads (`-XX:ConcGCThreads`).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Modern low-latency collectors (ZGC, Shenandoah, Go's tri-color GC) eliminate multi-second pauses by doing marking and compaction concurrently via read/write barriers.
Avoid trap: Setting `-Xms` and `-Xmx` too close to the live working set, starving the collector of free regions and causing 50%+ CPU spent in GC.
Avoid trap: Disabling Python's cyclic `gc` completely without verifying zero circular references in frameworks, causing slow memory leaks.

When to reach for it: Choose **generational copying/regional GC (G1GC, V8 Orinoco)** for general server workloads with high short-lived allocation rates (90%+ objects die in Eden) needing high throughput.
When to reach for it: Choose **concurrent compacting GC (JVM ZGC, Shenandoah)** when p99.9 latency SLAs demand <1 ms GC pauses even on 10 GB–1 TB+ heaps.

putItTogether.title: Putting Garbage Collection Algorithms Together
putItTogether.summary: Modern low-latency collectors (ZGC, Shenandoah, Go's tri-color GC) eliminate multi-second pauses by doing marking and compaction concurrently via read/write barriers.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Garbage Collection Algorithms before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Switching to `-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational` (JDK 21+) moves object relocation and reference remapping into concurrent load barriers, dropping p999 GC pauses to <0.4 ms at a ~5–10% throughput/CPU cost.
